- Best Meal Kit Overall Courtesy of Marley Spoon
Marley Spoon

### Meal Kit

Shop at

Marley Spoon

In the decade since it was introduced on American shores, the strength of the Martha Stewart–endorsed Marley Spoon meal delivery service has remained steadfast: It's the cooking.

The best individual meals I've cooked among the 20 or so kits I've tested in the past two years have come from Marley Spoon . A hearty Hungarian-influenced creamy mushroom chicken , a boldly Cajun-spiced whitefish, or a delicate eggplant parm. Those meals are still on the menu.

But Marley Spoon has also been evolving of late. Over the past year or two, the German-founded meal kit has added more menu items, more cosmopolitan meals with global flavors, and a greater variety of preparation times that now include a lot of 15-minute meals. It's done this without raising the price of the meal kit this year—no mean feat amid rising food and shipping costs.

The classic “Martha's Best” recipes are now augmented by meals that emphasize convenience and global flavors. A third of the menu is now prepared, ready-to-heat meals. I see more 15-minute dishes and tray oven bakes. Marley Spoon also seems to have broadened its international fare, with takes on a Moroccan-spiced apricot and beef tagine and Indian-influenced keema matar that's as easy to make as garam masala sloppy Joe.

Still, more than other meal kits, Marley remains devoted to classical cooking technique—the sort they teach in culinary school and on Martha Stewart's TV shows. This is no accident. When the German-founded meal kit arrived in the US, it did so with the cooking maven's endorsement and a lot of her recipes and techniques. Recipes often call for light seasoning throughout the process—not all at once. A kale and sausage soup, deeply savory, might be balanced with acid from a surprising splash of red wine vinegar.

Marley Spoon is more honest than most meal kits about the time it actually takes to cook a recipe. While your 15-minute meal might acccctually still require 20 minutes, it definitely won't take 30 or 40. There is one point of inconvenience with Marley, one that might help keep the company's prices from climbing: Unlike other top-line kits, Marley sends your ingredients jumbled in a box, which reduces packaging waste but also leaves you hunting for the right spice mix or dried ingredient. The meat sourcing also isn't as transparent as some kits.

Like Blue Apron and others, Marley Spoon has recently partnered with food delivery service Misfits Market after its previous US partner, FreshRealm, filed for Chapter 11 protection. I'll be testing and monitoring to make sure Marley keeps earning its spot at the top of this list. While maintaining value, Marley Spoon offers genuinely good cooking and acts as a little school in culinary techniques. Some other meal kits on this list might offer more flexibility. Marley offers a firm backbone.

- Best culinary technique on classic dishes
- Large selection of meals
- Excellent proteins and sourcing (Cento tomatoes!)
- Express and international meals take some shortcuts
- Boxes arrive disorganized
- Ready-to-heat meals aren't great
Home Chef

### Meal Kit

Shop at

Home Chef (Regular Plan)

Shop at

Home Chef (Larger Family Plan)

Home Chef lets you do pretty much whatever you want. Do you want two servings of two recipes, but eight servings of a third? No problem. Did you want to add an oven-ready steak meal for six to this week's order, and only this week's order? Also not a problem. Have a large family? Home Chef offers a cheaper family plan for batched family meals. Want fewer meals this week than your typical order? Each meal will cost a little more, but you can still cut back your order on the fly without canceling.

More than any other meal kit I've tested, Home Chef is optimized for convenience, down to the transparent plastic bags that house each meal's ingredients. The recipes are finely detailed, with easy-to-follow instructions. Nutrition and allergens are listed in even finer detail online. Each recipe is classed according to difficulty, and even the theoretically highfalutin’ “culinary collection” meals aren't hard to make or dauntingly culinary—mayhaps a stuffed chicken breast, perhaps some gnocchi.

It's not for nothing that WIRED previously listed Home Chef as the best meal kit for beginner chefs: The recipe instructions are full of little hand-holds and added advice. That said, the meals I've tried weren't quite as sophisticated and tasty as those you'll get from my top pick, Marley Spoon, nor as varied and interesting as HelloFresh. One “culinary” meal was basically a stuffed burger with seasoned fries.

But convenience, flexibility, and good administration count for a lot in this world. So do relatively low prices, at $10 a meal on most standard plans and $8 a plate for the kid-friendly family plan. If you've got a family life with meal demands that change from week to week—which is a lot of the people looking to meal kits to solve problems—Home Chef may be precisely the meal kit you need.

- Flexible meal planning for each week or meal
- Clear, well-written, helpful recipe cards
- Equal clarity about nutrition and allergens
- Some meals feel a bit under-seasoned
- Smaller selection than some
CookUnity

### Prepared Meals

Shop at

CookUnity

I'll put it simply: CookUnity is the only prepared-meal delivery service I've tried that has ever delivered a meal better than local restaurant takeout. Specifically, from the Seattle kitchen run by chef Gaurav Raj, I've tried multiple Indian gravies from butter chicken to chicken lababdar that tasted better than I could get at the Punjabi restaurant down the street.

Prepared meal delivery services promise a hunger-squelching holy grail: fresh meals, delivered to your door in a box that's ready to heat and eat, minus all the effort of actually cooking it. But my results from many other prepared-meal delivery services have been mixed. Indeed, some struggle to better the TV dinners they resemble. The reason CookUnity has been a big standout is its unique business model.

Most prepared meal plans come from a single big corporate kitchen. But CookUnity is more like a cross between a meal service and DoorDash. CookUnity enlists restaurant chefs, often big names like Jose Garces or Rick Bayless or Iron Chef contestants, to design recipes and hire cooks who make your meals out of regional commissary kitchens, and ship them never-frozen down the street. This model leads not just to quality but also to diversity of food.

Over two years of testing, I've tried multiple well-composed salads, a surprisingly wonderful truffled beef stroganoff, credible Filipino adobo, and Japanese-style katsu with curry that crisped up tantalizingly in an air fryer.

Menus, chefs, and (probably) results may vary depending on your region and your distance from the cooking hub. Hubs now include New York, Austin, Miami, Atlanta, Los Angeles, Seattle, Chicago, and Toronto. (See the delivery map to check whether CookUnity services your area.) I've had good results from the small Seattle hub, and WIRED reviewer Louryn Strampe said the adobo flank steak and rigatoni alla vodka she scored from the Chicago hub straight-up blew her mind.

Prep tends to happen one of two ways: Either you nuke it, or you can follow the chef's ideal heating instructions for a stovetop or oven meal to create optimal texture and flavor. After reheating, you might also stretch burrata cheese over your pasta or ladle cumin-forward sauce on your salmon. The meals are filling, the textures are spot-on, and the packaging is compostable and recyclable . Each meal lasts in the fridge between four and seven days from the date of delivery, through the miracle of modified atmosphere packaging .

After retesting CookUnity this year during warmer weather in Oregon, I found that my meals arrived at food-safe temperatures—no small feat, given that my meals drove in from four hours away in Seattle.

- The best prepared meal delivery I've tasted
- Global recipes from diverse chefs
- Microwaveable. But no microwave required
- Results can vary depending on chef or region
- In some small hubs, recipes might repeat
- Meal Kit With the Best Selection Courtesy of HelloFresh
HelloFresh

### Meal Kit

Shop at

HelloFresh

HelloFresh is pretty much synonymous with “meal kits.” It's the biggest of the services and among the oldest. It's become a global brand, available in 18 countries. Chances are, if you've tried a meal kit, it's among the first you tried. What's surprised me, though, is how much HelloFresh keeps improving since the first time I tried it five years ago: better sourcing and more cosmopolitan and modern recipes.

The brand has become a powerhouse of logistics. These days, you get seasonal or even regional ingredients, depending on where you live. Proteins are sourced from multigenerational, family-run meat purveyors. Each subscription box is also well-organized, with each recipe's ingredients portioned into labeled bags. All you need is pots, pans, a stove, and some basic oil- and salt- and butter-type kitchen staples.

Especially over the past year, HelloFresh has undergone a near-astonishing expansion of its menu. Where I live, more than 400 menu items are available each week, spanning a truly global range of cuisines. One day, I can find myself deep in a Gambian-inspired peanut stew. The next it's an aspirational Hainanese chicken feast , a simplified Thai-style green curry shrimp, Tex-Mex enchiladas slathered in cheese and ranchero sauce, or Guamanian-inflected chicken kelaguen. Or I can just make myself a salad, wrap, or sandwich.

This summer, HelloFresh has even offered single-order grill boxes in partnership with meat delivery service Good Chop , with 32 servings comprising burgers (six), dogs (eight), steaks (four), sausages (eight), and bacon (eight strips) for $80. (In my experience, the steaks and bacon were the two best selling points.)

Where possible, HelloFresh has even begun dabbling in seasonal ingredients, like conehead cabbage I charred on my grill last summer. In some areas, HelloFresh has even added regional dishes and ingredients. Honestly, it's an exercise in logistics that makes the nerd in me a little giddy. After criticism, including my own, the company added more rice to the rice meals last year. This said, shipping prices are up, and the per-serving price has hiked around 50 cents a serving this year as well—a tribute to the rising gas and food prices that have plagued 2026.

The global offerings don't make much claim to authenticity, mind you. Also, HelloFresh's 20-minute meals sometimes take as long as 40 minutes to make. But the offerings from HelloFresh look a lot like how people eat these days. They are bright, light, and lightly internationalized: with pan-Latin steak and rice bowls, beef stir-fried with ponzu and plum, Dutch-inspired orange Dijon chicken, Thai-style curries, and maybe some mango salsa atop a vaguely Southwest-y pork roast.

- Broad, cosmopolitan menu with more than 400 meal options per week
- Well-organized boxes, clear recipe instructions
- Transparent, often seasonal ingredient sourcing
- Recipes can take longer than expected
- Don't shoot for authenticity in global meals
- Healthiest Meal Delivery Service (With True Gluten-Free Options) Courtesy of Green Chef

Green Chef is first and foremost the organic arm of HelloFresh, assiduous enough that I got an apology note when they had to sub in non-organic roma tomatoes. Even in August, the most difficult time to ship perishable food, my herbs and veggies had nary a wilted leaf—a difficult and rare achievement, especially for fresh herbs like the parsley in the gremolata for a Turkish-spiced steelhead trout. There are fewer options overall than you'll find from HelloFresh's flagship kit, and Green Chef is among the more expensive meal kits. But the quality and diversity of ingredients do reflect this.

- Organic ingredients and independently validated gluten-free selections.
- Diverse food and sophisticated options
- Elegant simplicity in instructions.

Hungryroot has among the lowest prep times of any meal kit I've tested that isn't actually pre-prepped—perfect for your friend who “doesn't have time to cook" and instead finds their DoorDash budget ballooning. Usually, there's room left over in the plan to add some fresh fruit or a sweet treat. One detriment of this ultra-customized system is that you've got to get pretty far through the ordering process (and enter your credit card) before seeing your personal menu. Here's the online “cookbook” of potential menus , for those who'd like an early glimpse.

Blue Apron

### Meal Kit

Shop at

In the summer of 2025, America's OG meal kit brand, Blue Apron, underwent a transformation into a new model: No subscriptions required. So let’s say it’s Friday, and you'd like a kit so you can make some nice orecchiette and pork ragu next Tuesday, when your boss comes over for dinner (because life is, of course, a sitcom from the 1970s). You can just order it. Four days later, a bag will show up with recipe instructions and all the ingredients: ground pork, currants, fresh zucchini, all that. Rather have beef? You can sub that in. And you don't need to sign up for any minimum number of meals, nor subscribe and then need to cancel again.

This is a bit of a game changer for meal kits, frankly, though the scenario I just described would end up a bit expensive ($10 a serving, plus $10 shipping). And so Blue Apron also has a DoorDash-style loyalty model: Blue Apron Plus. You pay $10 a month, the price of shipping on a single order, and then shipping is free for the month. This means that if you order more than once a month, you save money by signing up. Price per meal has fanned out since the reboot, ranging from $8 a serving for lunchtime salads and wraps to $13 for hearty bakes and seafood plates. This allows you to choose meals based on budget.

This is an ambitious turnaround for a meal kit that WIRED reviewers had loved in the past before going through some bumps in the road under new ownership beginning in 2023 . So far I've had pretty good results. My most recent test included fun and internationalized recipes, like a crisp and lightly spicy bang bang chicken, bao bun burgers with shishito peppers, and za'atar-spiced salmon, plus an excellent and hearty shrimp and feta bake. Prep for most recipes hovered around 30 minutes. And on each, it was possible to sub out a main protein. WIRED reviewer Kat Merck tried Blue Apron's low-effort, assemble-and-bake meals and came away mostly impressed by the sourcing and quality of the ingredients—but also wondered whether the focus on simplicity led to compromises in some recipes. She couldn't bring herself to bake meat from raw on a harissa beef dish, per instructions, without first draining the grease. And so she cooked it in a skillet first.

There'd been a few ingredient hiccups in 2025 as the new plan rolled out, but this summer Blue Apron partnered with grocery delivery service Misfits Market as a new fulfillment and delivery partner—theoretically leading to more regional options and faster delivery. Blue Apron has also changed its packaging to be more eco-friendly. As this comes fully online, we'll be re-testing Blue Apron to see the results. Note that beyond main proteins, allergens and dietary restrictions can be a little difficult to navigate on Blue Apron's site.

- No subscription needed
- Easy prep, low cook times
- Fun, international meal options
- Allergens and nutritional info difficult to navigate

EveryPlate

### Meal Kit

Shop at

EveryPlate

With most plans at $7 a serving plus shipping, HelloFresh budget option EveryPlate remains the lowest-cost meal kit I've tested. And yet, this budget meal kit still uses the same proteins from local purveyors as HelloFresh’s much more expensive plan.

The secret is not skimping on calories or portions, but rather simplicity. EveryPlate's meals derive their flavors from a small set of ingredients, and a single sauce or herb or spice mix—or perhaps some citrus cross-utilized as both juice and zest. Ingredients also tend to be cross-utilized quite a bit, which doubles as good cooking.

In a test this year, I made myself a fun Tex-Mex-style “quesabirria” with a chili-style spice paste; a hearty plate of pork chops with thyme and shallots; and a ground-turkey rice bowl that relied on ginger, garlic, and a mix of soy glaze and citric ponzu sauce.

HelloFresh's low price makes it the only meal plan I've tried that wouldn't require any particular adjustment in my grocery budget—at least for two people. And yet, this budget meal plan from HelloFresh is somehow able to offer dinners that even your judgy mom-in-law would recognize as a balanced dinner.

This year's pork chop meal in particular is the sort of meat-and-two supper that I probably took too much for granted when I was a child. Pan-seared chops. Crispy-leafed brussels sprouts baked in the oven. Fresh mashed potatoes. But what elevated the meal from basic staple to weekday extravagance was a thoughtful shallot-garlic-cream pan sauce, cooked with fresh thyme in the juices from the pork I'd just finished searing. The sauce was rich, complex, aromatic, and just enough outside my usual repertoire that I felt like I'd learned a useful secret.

The laundry list of staples you're expected to have in your fridge for EveryPlate is a little longer than with more expensive kits and includes flour and eggs. The box of ingredients is not as organized as HelloFresh's. The menu is significantly shorter than HelloFresh's at about 35 options, but still competitive with many meal delivery services. While the meals skew more basic than adventurous, I came away impressed by the simple good taste and economy on offer from EveryPlate, at a price that would not stretch a lot of household budgets.

My colleague Molly Higgins, who eats no meat, had a good experience with EveryPlate's shorter menu of vegetarian options this spring and was able to secure a week's worth of food for less than she ends up spending on groceries in New York. Sure, you may want to fill out a meal by adding your own rice to supplement Korean-inflected beef or pork with squash and carrots. ( A great rice cooker makes this easy .) This adds up to an economical meal, one you might appreciate on a Tuesday when you're out of other ideas.

Best budget meal delivery service for large families: Marley Spoon's lower-cost meal kit, Dinnerly , was WIRED's former budget pick. It's still a good, affordable pick for small families, if not quite as low-cost as EveryPlate. But for large families (six portions), it's almost certainly the best budget option at a mere $6 a meal, with a much larger selection of recipes. Compared to my testing last year, Dinnerly's recipes have grown lighter, more sophisticated, and maybe a little smarter: a za'atar chicken recipe here, a Mediterranean-inflected pork tenderloin or lemon-butter shrimp there. Often it feels like you're getting my top-pick kit, Marley Spoon, at a discount. The difference shows up mostly in the simplicity of Dinnerly's ingredient list, usually comprising a simple herb or spice accent rather than a complicated medley of flavors. $6 a serving for six-serving meals.

- Simple, hearty, low-cost meals

### Prepared Meal Delivery Subscription

Tempo

According to everyone I know taking a GLP-1 medication for weight loss or diabetes management, the drive to seek out delicious food just isn't what it used to be. What has not changed is the utilitarian need to get enough protein, in a reasonable form, balanced against other health considerations. Does this not sound romantic? It mostly isn't. But if hunger doesn't move you like it used to, it's extra important for your food to taste good enough that you actually want to eat it.

Enter Tempo by Home Chef , a never-frozen, prepared meal service that offers a selection of around 30 meals each week. As many as two-thirds of these meals are marked “protein-packed,” with more than 30 grams of protein. And at least 10 of these are GLP-1-balanced, per a dietitian. What you'll get: sufficient proteins, not too many carbs, no other funny stuff.

Tempo's proteins are well-managed, if unexciting. But the meals were easy, nutritious, balanced, and comforting, without relying on a pile of unhealthy sodium and carbs to be palatable. At $12 a meal, Tempo's pricing is about par for the course for prepared meals.

WIRED reviewer Kat Merck, who tested the GLP-1-balanced meals, found the portions appropriate for those on the medication and appreciated that the meals offered her the proteins she needs to maintain muscle mass even while chemically un-hungry. Just note: You may end up with a lot of chicken and a lot of fish. Both Merck and I were happy to see the occasional chicken thigh, and not just breast. Thighs are better, for the record.

Note that for pure protein-loading and management of your macros, a no-nonsense option is Fuel Meals (see below), which has almost no sodium and more than 40 grams of protein per meal.

- Mostly nutritious, balanced meals
- Caters to GLP-1 and high-protein diets
- Proteins are supsrisingly moist and tender
- Anyone with eating restrictions is in for lots of chicken
- Veggies can be soggy
- Meals are relatively low-calorie, which could lead to quicker hunger
## More Meal Kits I Liked

Sunbasket

Sunbasket (~$16 per serving) : Sunbasket focuses heavily on fresh, organic ingredients and offers a whole lot of variety in its menus. Its recipes are attentive to saucing, and to basic good cooking techniques such as deglazing. Like Hungryroot, it also offers breakfasts and snacks to supplement meal options with little extras such as coconut yogurt and sous-vide egg bites. The meal kit also lets you filter out allergen-containing items. WIRED reviewer Louryn Strampe loved the flexibility and add-ons. During my most recent test, I enjoyed an excellent Greek chicken and orzo salad dish—and, wonder of wonders, the advertised prep time was actually the actual prep time (about 30 minutes). The focus on organic ingredients does make Sunbasket one of the more expensive meal kit options, and the annual Thanksgiving meal kit was a lovely and welcome extravagance at $200 .

Gardencup ($11 to $15 a serving) : Gardencup is a little like having the whole menu of Sweetgreen sent to your house or office, except in cylindrical form. Basically, you pick out premade salads, soups, and snacks, and they come in little cups—fresh, lovely, crisp, and ready to eat. I found it to be a great way to keep myself eating healthy when there's no time to cook at the office (or the home office), which is typically when DoorDash or freezer-meal temptations run wild. It remains among the healthiest prepared food delivery options I know. I even tested Gardencup as a salad option during a cyclospora parasite scare, in part because I missed salad and because Gardencup could attest that it did not use lettuce from any of the suspected sources of the outbreak. The salads remained delicious and delivered a shocking amount of protein in options with meat. But variety of options is not a strong suit. A slackened focus on local sourcing, plus limited transparency on sourcing—Gardencup will disclose only that it sources its greens in the salad belt from Salinas, California, to Yuma, Arizona—has kept Gardencup in my honorable mentions.

Factor

Factor ($13 to $17 a serving) : Factor is a prepared-meal delivery plan run by HelloFresh, with ready-to-eat meals that look a lot like TV dinners. But there's a twist: The trays have never been frozen. They were made fresh in a commissary kitchen and were shipped out with cold packs, yielding a result that's kind of like restaurant leftovers. Consistently, Factor ranks among the best-tasting prepared meal plans I've tested, especially when I shrug off directions and use an air fryer to reheat my meals instead of a microwave. Proteins and high-protein meals are a strong suit. Proteins maintain their texture quite well, especially a truffled filet mignon I couldn't believe I microwaved. Still, some meals, especially carb-avoidant or keto meals, are oddly mushy, while meals centered on proteins and whole starches, like potatoes or rice, alongside veggies like green beans or brussels sprouts, tended to fare quite well. So did stir-fry-style meals. My gluten-free colleague, Scott Gilbertson, wrote that he had the best luck with Factor's Mexican fare . I do wish Factor would shed its reliance on the microwave: When I went off-script and used a Ninja Crispi air fryer or convection oven, I had much better results than with the nuker. But non-air-fryer ovens do not seem to offer the same improvement. Like many ready-to-eat meals, it's a bit more expensive than the kits you cook yourself. Oh, and as a bonus? Factor has a really, truly delicious selection of nutrient-amped juice bottles and elderberry “shots.” I could pretty much subsist on their probiotic cucumber-pineapple green juice.

Fuel Meals

Fuel Meals ($14 to $15 a serving) : Fuel Meals are a no-nonsense, no-fluff, no-added-ingredients, pure-protein-packed nutritive meal plan, with many meals paleo-friendly. Some of Fuel's meals had as few as five ingredients, consisting of essentially the macronutrients themselves plus a modicum of oil and salt. A large percentage of meals are marked gluten-free or dairy-free. Does all this mean less flavor? It can. The meals are also often not beautiful, dominated by a large and no-fuss serving of protein. But Fuel's meal service offers an admirable focus, especially for those bulking up or watching carbs. Meals are substantive, usually topping 600 calories and 40 grams of protein without added sugar or fatty dairy or carb-heavy filler. I feel like if I wore tank tops more often, this is what I'd eat.

Wildgrain

Wildgrain ($13 to $17 per loaf or box of pastries) : This is less a meal delivery service than a way to step up a home meal. Wildgrain is a monthly delivery bread box: You receive par-baked bread and pastries from small bakeries all over the country. This is pretty much the same process that likely happens at local restaurants when your warm bread basket comes out: It's not quite as high-quality as you'd get direct from an artisan bakery, if you live in places with artisan bakeries. But it's also as fresh as it gets, and I had a very good experience testing the box in October 2025, in particular, with sourdough breads perfect for large meals with houseguests. You finish the baking at home, so what you have at the end is ultra-fresh baked bread, biscuits, doughnuts, or scones that are still warm and crisp from the oven. A Wildgrain subscription arrives as a monthly box, filled with four, six, or 12 items that might range from a full sourdough loaf or fresh-made pasta to a pack of six doughnuts or four large croissants. Basically, you build your own box each month , choosing from among healthy sourdough or pasta and decadent pastries.

Thistle ($12 to $15 per meal) : A prior top pick for solo diners with individually prepared dishes that require little to no prep, Thistle is mostly a plant-based meal kit—but there's a $3 option to add sustainable meats to any otherwise vegan meal. It's also so local and seasonal that the West and East Coasts have different menus, and the whole middle of the country, except Chicago, gets none. ( You can check your zip code here to see if you can get delivery.) WIRED reviewer Adrienne So has used Thistle as a means to get herself to eat more vegetables, and thus avoid a life of rickets and/or scurvy. Portions are generous enough to split among meals, and in a nice turn for those who hate having to dispose of boxes, Thistle's drivers will pick up the cooler bag that housed last week's meal and replace it with a new one full of food. Vegan tester Molly Higgins's favorite meals from Thistle were a whirlwind of textures, including a Mexican-inspired corn and poblano chile salad with adobo pinto beans and a chilled lemongrass-accented rice noodle bowl that mixed spice, tang, crisply fresh veggies, and deep umami from mushrooms and seaweed. She still dreams about it sometimes. Breakfasts are available at a lower cost, as low as $9.

Tovala

Tovala (~$9 to $15 a serving) : It's not every day you get to try something that feels super new. Tovala offers perhaps the most ambitious solution to ready-to-heat and prepared meal delivery I've seen: The meal kits come with an oven! In contrast to the sogginess of many prepared meals, Tovala's recipes come in little foil pans with recipes custom-designed for a little steam oven. The results are often delicious—as was the case during my testing with a sweet chili–glazed salmon with pickled veg and noodles—and the QR code scanning function makes each recipe seamless to cook. Stick with the meal plan for six weeks, and in the bargain you get a quite affordable and powerful little convection oven, toaster, and steamer. A previous flaw was that Tovala only offered single-serve meals. But as of early 2026, at least four or five meals a week offer two to four servings, making the meal delivery service much more useful to families and couples—and much more economical on a per-serving basis. But not that it's also one of the most sodium-filled meal services I've tested.

Gobble

Gobble ($17 a serving) : Formerly the top pick for fast-cooked meals, Gobble previously wowed with speed-demon dishes that also offered interesting and worldly flavors. Indeed, the most recent test included Caribbean rondon, an Indonesian peanut curry stir-fry, and steak vierge. But while the flavors have stayed interesting, the focus on fast cooking appears to have waned since my colleague Louryn Strampe tested Gobble. Cook time estimates aren't printed on the recipe cards, but meals took as long as 30 minutes. For now, Hungryroot has taken the fast-cooking crown. For small households, Gobble is also among the most expensive kits. At most portions, prices approach $17 a serving plus shipping.

Nurture Life ($6 to $7 per serving) : Nurture Life is like a restaurant kids' menu, in ready-to-eat meal kit form. We loved the idea behind this fresh-made, never-frozen delivery meal plan when we tested it a few years back: a bunch of toddler- and slightly bigger kid-friendly meals, from mac and cheese to spaghetti and meatballs to myriad variations on the chicken nugget. The meal prices have dipped to reasonable levels of late, meaning it's likely due for a retest—and each plate contains vegetables alongside the greatest hits.

Veestro ($7 to $14 per serving) : WIRED reviewer Louryn Strampe enjoyed Veestro as a ready-to-eat vegan option, with premade meals delivered fresh, but with freezable options so you can have extra meals on hand in a pinch. The service offers a number of filters for other dietary requirements, and satisfying taste and texture—which is not always a guarantee on ready-to-eat meals. Veestro has updated its menu and offerings since the last time WIRED tested, including a number of snacky soup offerings. The online menu interface , allowing you to sort by ingredients and filter out unwanted ones, is among the best I've seen.

Splendid Spoon ($9 to $13 per serving) : Splendid Spoon is a nutrition delivery kit that offers a plethora of plant-based smoothies, soups, bowls, noodles, and shots. Everything here is natural, plant-based, and free of gluten or GMOs, including spaghetti and plant-based “meatballs.” WIRED reviewer Louryn Strampe has a big yen for the smoothies in particular ($10 apiece), but wasn't quite prepared for the intensity of a lemon juice shot that comes as part of a five-pack of dense 3-ounce superfoods.

ModifyHealth's Braised Beef (top) and Paprika Salmon (bottom)

ModifyHealth ($10 to $13 per serving) : The idea behind ModifyHealth is that food can be medicine. Sometimes, I'll admit, it tasted like it was designed purely for nutrition rather than flavor. ModifyHealth is a prepared meal delivery service tailored to people who need a heart-healthy, low-carb, or low-FODMAP diet to avoid dire digestive or health consequences. GLP-1 weight-loss plans are also available for people with diabetes or others. Gluten-free meals are attested to be made in an entirely gluten-free facility. The meals were simple, benign, and low-sodium but also sometimes a little soggy—a common problem with prepared meals. The plastic top of the packaging was also difficult to disengage from the base of each meal tray—a problem when the plastic is hot after a turn in the microwave. But here's what I do like: The meals are carefully tailored with consultation from dietitians to help people for whom food can be a source of fear or pain. An additional service, offering one-on-one dietitian consultation, can be covered by many insurance plans. ModifyHealth also offers a free consultation for those just trying to figure out which diet plan is right for them. For those with IBS in particular, this remains the most focused food plan I've seen.

Daily Harvest (prices vary) : Daily Harvest is another ready-to-eat meal delivery service specializing in dietary restrictions: plant-based, plus gluten- and dairy-free. Smoothies feature, as do harvest bowls, pastas, and grains. Calories are low. Ingredients are often inventive. The meal's a lifesaver for the solo vegan eater without time to prep a meal, and WIRED vegan reviewer Molly Higgins appreciated that the meals mostly relied on the natural flavors of the vegetables themselves, accented with flavors like curry and lemongrass. As with a lot of frozen meals, however, texture wasn't a strong suit in the ready-to-heat meals. The ready-to-blend smoothies are great, though.

## A Meal Kit I Don’t Recommend

Sakara Life ($30+ per serving) : Sakara Life offers plant-based weekly menus in fresh, prepared portions, with greens, flavorful sauces, all-organic ingredients, and textural add-ons like seeds or berries. But it's among the most expensive meal plans we've tested, and neither WIRED reviewer who tried it has really cottoned to the thing. Tester Louryn Strampe questioned the science on health claims for detoxes and cleanses , while calling Sakara “egregiously expensive” and full of “bitter veggies and tart fruits.” Vegan tester Molly Higgins, meanwhile, said Sakara Life's tinctures and metabolism supplements didn't agree with her system, and that the mostly raw-food plan made her long for “human food.”

## Frequently Asked Questions

Are Meal Delivery Services Worth It?

If you're talking raw materials by the pound—meat, zucchini, rice, noodles—meal kits will, of course, cost more than buying food at grocery stores. It's a service, after all, with added value above simple ingredient cost. Unless you've got quite expensive taste, you'll easily be able to make delicious meals at home for less than the $7 to $14 a serving that a meal kit will cost. That said, this doesn't necessarily mean that meal kits are expensive for what they offer. I conducted an experiment, trying to re-create four different meal-kit meals by going to my local grocery store —buying every ingredient provided by the meal kit. Turns out, if you don't have the right sauces and spices at home already, it's very difficult to re-create these tasty meals at grocery stores for less than they cost from a meal kit, in part because you'll most likely have to buy full containers of sauces and spices instead of preportioned ingredients,

So, is HelloFresh worth it compared to a grocery store? Caveats are in order: For staple ingredients and spices you'll use in multiple recipes, the grocery store is, of course, cheaper. Once you buy a container of paprika for an individual recipe, it will also be there for future recipes, whereas meal-kit spices are portioned for the meal. So the real answer is that meal kits can be a quite economical way of trying out a new recipe, or a new style of cooking, without larding up your fridge with condiments you won't use again. For ingredients you'd use less commonly, a meal kit can reduce waste and spoilage, and maybe even compete on price for an individual meal.

If your comparison point is takeout, well, the best meal delivery services on this list will almost certainly be cheaper and more nutritious. I've found that a meal kit in the fridge tends to be a good motivator to cook a nutritive meal—and thus can save me both the money and the cholesterol.

To really save on cost, some people like to keep testing out the trial offers and discounts. Much like mattress-in-a-box companies, meal kit companies usually have a running promotion. Usually this takes the form of a trial discount price that'll drop your cost by half or more on the first box, in hopes you'll like the service enough to keep it on at full price.

For me, a meal kit a few times a week ends up balancing out well: It's a motivating factor to eat better, and it means that when I do go to the grocery store, I can do so less mindlessly and more purposefully, given that I've got a few meals' worth of ingredients in the fridge. It's also had the side effect of broadening my culinary toolkit, keeping me from getting stuck in the same ruts.

That said, it's a set grocery expense and not necessarily a small one. I do get tired of tossing or recycling cold packs and boxes. And depending on the time of year, I often prefer shopping in person for what's seasonal and local, when produce is at its peak—an experience you don't get from a meal kit, or from grocery delivery for that matter. If you're cooking for a bigger household, meal kits can also lose their utility quite quickly. A convenient option for two can become a much larger expense for a family of four or six.

Can I Pause a Meal Kit Service When I Go on Vacation?

Pretty much every meal kit I've tested has an option to pause subscriptions—and there's no particular limit to how often you can do this. The main thing is to be sure that you've canceled with enough lead time. Some services let you cancel or pause delivery as late as the Friday before a Monday delivery. HelloFresh requires five days' notice. Marley Spoon, at least where I live, required six days. Some, like Hungryroot, may lock in next week's order as early as the previous Monday, depending on where you live. Read your terms of service, and act accordingly.

For those with more variable schedules, the service I'd probably recommend is Blue Apron , which changed its model last year and no longer locks in delivery each week. You'll have to remember to order a box each week, which can be done where I am with four days' notice.

How to Optimize Meal Kits

Don't order too many meals per week: You know the old John Lennon line: Life is what happens when you're busy, out eating a random burrito, then thinking guiltily about the meal kit at home in your fridge. Aspirations are great, but don't order more meals than you're likely to make, or you'll be sad. Err on the side of caution. Order just enough meals per week that making yourself a recipe from your HelloFresh or Home Chef box is still a delight and a convenience and an overall boon to your life—not an obligation. For me, a somewhat improvisational and impulsive person, three meals a week is the sweet spot. The prospect of a few easy meals usually saves me from an impulse weeknight DoorDash.

Make room in your fridge: Meal kits take the place of a lot of grocery shopping. But they're also a lot of food, and a lot to keep organized. What I like to do is clear a tall enough space in my fridge to put the whole meal kit box in the fridge, after pulling out the cold packs: This way, I'm not left worrying about which groceries belong to the meal kit, and I won't lose any ingredients. I can just pull the whole box out when I want to make a meal. That said, some plans like Home Chef, HelloFresh, and Green Chef are very good at organizing each meal into its own separate bag. An added bonus from these more organized plans is that you'll be able to use less space in your fridge. Over time, this will matter.

Check the recipe cards to make sure you have everything you need to make a recipe: Most meal kits expect that you'll have certain staple ingredients in your home, usually including oil and butter. Recipes also have requirements for cookware. Check this before you start a recipe. Nothing worse than realizing you need an absentee stick of butter on step 5, with carrots already browning in the oven.

Remember, you owe nothing to the recipe: Meal kit services hire recipe developers, and on the best meal kits, these chefs have spent a lot of time optimizing each recipe. But you owe them nothing— nothing ! Add spices, change steps, season food when you want to season it. Meal kits can teach you a lot about how to make a good meal and shake you out of tired culinary routines. But it's your meal. Make it how you like. Have fun.

How Do I Test Meal Kits?

Chances are, wherever you are, whatever week it is, I'm testing a meal kit. I constantly cycle through various meal kits, testing and retesting each of my top picks at least once a year—and often multiple times per year.

Unlike other news sites that task many staffers with testing a different meal kit apiece—making direct comparisons difficult—I endeavor to test and retest all of WIRED's top picks at least once a year. I check in on other meal kits as relevant, especially when each meal delivery service changes its format or expands to new offerings.

I order at least four meals a week from each meal delivery service when possible. I prepare meals according to instructions, and see how well it goes. (Or, if I deviated from instructions out of horror or curiosity or a simple sense of culinary propriety, I note this and tell you why.)

I check my own prep times against the advertised prep times (rarely an exercise in honesty!), and take note of any inconsistencies, vagueness, or frustration in the recipe card instructions. If a meal kit needlessly recommends a nonstick pan, I like it less, especially if the recipe says I should heat said pan before adding food—or if it later makes mention of browned fond in the recipe. Nonstick isn't cast iron or carbon; there's no fond. If rice portions are too small, I also say so.

I check for the quality and freshness of the produce, and do the same for the meat. Where possible, I look into where the meat was sourced, and check on the reputation, safety, and standards of the meat suppliers. If a meal kit swears it's gluten-free, I check on this—calling certifying organizations where relevant.

I usually try to order as varied a menu as possible. When relevant, I might check in on gluten-free meals, a seafood item, a vegetarian item, and white and dark meat items. I might also test a Midwestern-style hot dish or Southern meat-and-two alongside meals that draw (or attempt to draw) from global inspirations. Sometimes I test the same meal kit multiple times for different dietary needs, or call in multiple testers to do so. WIRED's vegan tester, Molly Higgins , often tests the same meal kit I do but with a different focus.

# Schweden setzt Geflüchteten unter Druck: Ein absurdes Vorgehen

## Schweden setzt Geflüchteten unter Druck : Ein absurdes Vorgehen

Der Russe Aleksey Makarov lebt seit 2011 in Malmö und kämpfte bei der ukrainischen Armee. In Schweden droht ihm nun die Widerrufung seines Geflüchtetenstatus.

26.11.2026

14:28 Uhr

teilen

Diesen Artikel teilen

Aleksey Makarov kämpfte gegen die russische Armee Foto: privat

Von

„Also, als im Februar 2022 der vollumfängliche Krieg begann, beschloss ich, in die Ukraine zu fahren, um die ukrainische Gesellschaft vor der russischen Invasion zu schützen.“ So beginnt Aleksey Makarov, der im Krieg den Soldatennamen „Shved“ („Schwede“) annahm, bei einem Gespräch mit der taz seine Geschichte.

Der 38 Jahre alte russische Staatsbürger mit aufgewecktem Blick, der sich selbst als Anarchisten und Internationalisten versteht, geriet schon als 17-jähriger Geschichtsstudent in Moskau in Konflikt mit Putins Russland. Als politischer Gefangener verbrachte er zwei Jahre in Lagerhaft, lebte anschließend von 2009 bis 2011 in der Ukraine, wo er unter dem prorussischen Präsidenten Janukowitsch erneut im Gefängnis landete. 2011 erhielt er Asyl in Schweden, er lernte die Sprache, studierte und jobbte als Postbote und Zugschaffner.

Doch mit der russischen Invasion änderte sich alles für ihn. Ab Sommer 2022 kämpfte er als Freiwilliger auf der ukrainischen Seite – gegen die Armee seines eigenen Heimatlandes, und zunächst ohne Vertrag oder Sold. „Glück liegt nicht im Geld, sondern darin, gegen den russischen Faschismus zu kämpfen“, sagt Makarov abgeklärt.

In der ukrainischen Armee war er Stürmer und Maschinengewehrschütze, bis Ende Februar 2023 zunächst bei der 95. separaten Fallschirmjäger-Sturmbrigade. Nach einem kurzen Aufenthalt in Schweden war er danach bis Sommer 2024 Teil des „Sibirischen Bataillons“, einer dem ukrainischen Militärgeheimdienst unterstellten Einheit speziell für russische Staatsbürger.

„Es war nicht einfach nur eine Teilnahme am Krieg, sondern ein politisches Projekt mit anarchistischer Ausrichtung: der Schutz der ukrainischen Gesellschaft vor der russischen Aggression“, erklärt Makarov seine Motivation. Sein Bataillon habe riskante Aufgaben erfüllt: Einsätze in der Region Donezk und im März 2024 gar eine Operation in der russischen Region Belgorod, während der er an seiner rechten Hand verwundet wurde.

## Er gefährde Schwedens Sicherheit

Im August 2024 reiste Makarov zurück nach Schweden. Zum einen, weil sein Geflüchteten-Reisedokument abgelaufen sei, schildert er, vor allem aber zur Genesung: „Im Grunde ist diese auch heute noch nicht abgeschlossen, sie wird nie enden, denn an meiner rechten Hand habe ich fast keine Beweglichkeit in drei Fingern mehr.“

Jetzt kämpft er nicht nur mit gesundheitlichen Problemen, sondern auch mit den schwedischen Behörden. Im April 2023 beantragte Makarov die schwedische Staatsbürgerschaft und im Dezember 2024 außerdem ein neues Reisedokument für Geflüchtete. „All diese Verfahren dauerten sehr lange“, erklärt er. „Zunächst wurde mir im August des Jahres 2025 die schwedische Staatsbürgerschaft wegen einer angeblichen Gefahr für die nationale Sicherheit verweigert. Und am 7. September dieses Jahres erhielt ich dann die Ablehnung meines Antrags auf einen Flüchtlingspass.“

Bei einer Vorladung bei der Migrationsbehörde im Juni 2026 sei ihm die Entscheidung des schwedischen Sicherheitsdienstes (Säpo) verlesen worden. Dabei handelt es sich um den schwedischen nationalen Geheimdienst. „Darin hieß es, ich hätte im Ausland Aktivitäten ausgeübt, die die Sicherheit Schwedens gefährden“, erinnert sich Makarov. Inwiefern er das angeblich tut, was ihm konkret unterstellt wird, wurde ihm jedoch nie erklärt. Die taz konnte die entsprechenden Dokumente der schwedischen Behörden, die diese Makarov zukommen ließen, einsehen und Makarovs Darstellung bestätigen.

Ohne ein gültiges Reisedokument kann er Schweden nicht mehr verlassen. Auch fürchtet er eine weitere Verschlechterung seiner Lage. „Es besteht die Möglichkeit einer Abschiebung nach Russland, aber die Wahrscheinlichkeit ist äußerst gering. Allerdings könnte ich ohne Papiere enden oder auf unbestimmte Zeit inhaftiert werden.“

## Marakov legt Berufung ein

Makarovs Anwalt, Miran Kakaee, erklärte gegenüber der taz, sein Mandant habe gegen die Entscheidung der schwedischen Migrationsbehörde Berufung eingelegt. Man erwarte das Urteil jeden Moment und werde gegebenenfalls Möglichkeiten für internationale Beschwerden prüfen. Kakaee hält es für denkbar, dass als Nächstes rechtliche Schritte folgen könnten, um Makarovs Geflüchtetenstatus und im schlimmsten Fall seine Aufenthaltserlaubnis zu widerrufen. „Es ist offensichtlich, dass die Behörden versuchen, die Situation für Aleksey zu verschärfen“, so Kakaee.

Der Anwalt verwies auch auf andere Fälle in Schweden, bei denen mit Verweis auf Stellungnahmen des Sicherheitsdienstes Geflüchteten Dokumente verweigert würden. Die Stellungnahmen würden in der Regel wenig Informationen preisgeben, sodass sie sich von den Betroffenen auch schwer anfechten ließen.

„In Alekseys Fall haben wir, obwohl wir es aufgrund fehlender Informationen nicht genau wissen, Grund zu der Annahme, dass sein Aufenthalt in der Ukraine die Ursache für die Ablehnung ist. Das Einmalige an seinem Fall ist, dass seine Handlungen tatsächlich klar, könnte man sagen, im Einklang mit den nationalen Sicherheitsinteressen Schwedens stehen“, so Kakaee. Das Vorgehen der schwedischen Behörden sei absurd. Schweden, seit 2024 Nato-Mitglied , steht der Ukraine bei und unterstützt das überfallene Land militärisch und humanitär.

Die taz stellte schriftliche Anfragen sowohl an den Sicherheitsdienst als auch an die schwedische Migrationsbehörde. Doch beide antworteten wenig konkret und verwiesen jeweils auf die Zuständigkeit der anderen Institution. Der Sicherheitsdienst schrieb, er könne sich nicht zu bestimmten Personen äußern, die Gegenstand von Entscheidungen der schwedischen Migrationsbehörde seien. Die Fälle würden der Geheimhaltung unterliegen.

Derweil antwortete die schwedische Migrationsbehörde auf die Anfrage der taz: „Die Gründe für diese Einschätzung sind in der Entscheidung dargelegt, über die Herr Makarov informiert wurde. Wir müssen Sie bitten, sich zwecks weiterer Erläuterungen zu den Gründen für dessen Einschätzung an den schwedischen Sicherheitsdienst zu wenden.“ Doch dieser reagierte auf eine Rückfrage der taz nicht mehr.

articleBody:
# Zu viel versprochen: Warum Ubisoft wegen eines Piratenspiels verklagt wird

## Zu viel versprochen: Warum Ubisoft wegen eines Piratenspiels verklagt wird

Yves Guillemot, Boss von Ubisoft, nannte „Skull and Bones“ ein „AAAA“-Spiel, also ein besonderes Top-Game. Dagegen gingen Spieler vor. Vor Gericht erklärten die Anwälte des Konzerns, was von der Aussage zu halten ist: nichts.

Die Juristen des französischen Spieleriesen Ubisoft haben eine vielzitierte Aussage von Firmenchef Yves Guillemot über ein neues Game vor Gericht als reine Werbeübertreibung eingestuft. Das berichtet der Journalist Stephen Totilo in seinem Newsletter Game File. Konkret sprachen die Anwälte von „Puffery“ – also von einer allgemeinen, subjektiven Anpreisung ohne konkrete Tatsachenbehauptung, wie sie in der Werbung üblich ist. Guillemot hatte den Titel „Skull and Bones“, ein Piratenabenteuer, als „AAAA“-Titel bezeichnet, also als besonders hochwertig. Wie sich herausstellte, war es das Game aber nicht.

Hintergrund der Affäre ist eine Klage aus dem Jahr 2025. Ein US-Amerikaner warf Ubisoft vor, Verbraucher mit den Aussagen zu „Skull and Bones“ in die Irre geführt und damit gegen das Verbraucherschutzgesetz des Bundesstaats Kansas verstoßen zu haben. Weit kam die Klage jedoch nicht: Der Kläger scheiterte mit mehreren Anträgen, seit September ist das Verfahren eingestellt.

## „Quadruple-A“ für 70 US-Dollar

Dennoch zeigen die nun veröffentlichten Gerichtsaussagen, wie Ubisoft offenbar wirklich dachte. Guillemot hatte die Formulierung im Februar 2024 in einer Telefonkonferenz zu den Quartalszahlen benutzt. Dort verteidigte er den Preis von 70 US-Dollar für das Piratenspiel. Auf die Frage, ob ein Free-to-Play-Modell nicht besser zu einem Live-Service-Game passe – also zu einem Titel, der über Jahre mit neuen Inhalten versorgt wird –, verwies er auf den Umfang.

articleBody:
Built in 1840, this one-room School House served as the educational center for all of the first to eighth grade children in the Hockanum area, later serving only up to sixth grade. This was one of several school houses serving small neighborhood communities around Hadley.

A 1647 Massachusetts law required all towns with 50 or more families to hire a teacher to instruct their children in reading and writing. Parents and students contributed to their school in the form of money, goods, supplies, and chores.

These were one-room schoolhouses, on land that was usually donated. Most schools had one book, the "New England Primer," that was used to teach the alphabet, syllables, and prayer.

The last class to go through this school was in 1933. By then, it was more economical to bus students to the center of town than to keep the neighborhood school houses open.

Along with the outhouse next to it, the Hockanum School House was, and still is, taken care of by the Hockanum community.

articleBody:
# Draining peatlands is responsible for a few percent of our global warming

Much of the focus for human-caused climate change is on fossil fuels, which are creating most of our problems. But land use change is also a large component of the story, accounting for about one-third of total historical CO 2 emissions. Deforestation plays a major role here, but practices like draining wetlands also factor in. Exactly how much of our history of eliminating wetlands has contributed to warming is challenging to figure out. But thanks to new sources of data that measure emissions from today’s surviving wetlands, it’s possible to put a better number on it.

A new study led by Jevan Yu at MIT focuses on peatlands—environments like bogs and fens where organic matter accumulates into thick layers of material. Some 600 billion tons of carbon are held in these vast stores of peat, which is more than you can find in all the world’s living vegetation, the researchers note.

Because these areas are permanently inundated, any oxygen in the water is quickly used up, leaving the job of decaying all that organic matter to anaerobic bacteria that work much more slowly and don’t digest everything. So instead of seeing organic carbon turning into the CO 2 gas released by aerobic bacteria, in peatlands, a subset of it gradually turns into methane gas. Methane is an even more potent greenhouse gas than CO 2 itself and ultimately gets oxidized into CO 2 . That means there’s a little trade-off from peatlands—most of the carbon they have is kept out of the atmosphere, but the carbon that does escape does so as methane.

Many peatlands have been drained by digging ditches that let water flow out to repurpose the land for agriculture or other uses. That lowers the water level, supplying oxygen to the exposed peat and ringing the aerobic bacteria dinner bell. Methane emissions get turned down, and CO 2 emissions get turned way up.

## History re: peats

The researchers used recent studies that measure gas emissions from peatlands to build a global model that estimated CO 2 and methane release as the water level drops. The two gases respond differently to a given drop in water level, and CO 2 in particular responds differently depending on where in the world the bog is located. Using reconstructions of water-level changes due to historical peatland drainage, the team ran their model starting in 1800.

The simplest way to represent the climate impact of both CO 2 and methane changes was to calculate the change in Earth’s energy budget—the strength of the greenhouse effect, in other words. They calculated the total effect in 2020 at about +83 milliwatts per square meter of the Earth’s surface from the CO 2 emissions, and about -9 milliwatts per square meter from the reduced methane emissions, for a total effect of +73 mW. That is 2.7 percent of the total human-caused change in Earth’s energy budget. (With the error bars on all these numbers, it’s 1.8–3.6 percent.)

Or to look at it another way, it means that around 4 percent of all the carbon that was buried in peatlands is now in the atmosphere.

Regionally, over half of the total CO 2 came from Europe, almost a quarter came from Southeast Asia, and only 14 percent came from North America. The timing is quite different, as well, with the contribution from Southeast Asia only jumping up in the last few decades.

Draining a peatland only starts the process of releasing carbon, though. So that means past land-use change will still be producing emissions in the future. To examine this, the researchers also ran their model forward to 2100.

If peatland water levels were simply held constant from 2020 on, the total change in Earth’s energy budget would nearly double, from 73 to 138 milliwatts per square meter by 2100. Moderate restoration of peatland water levels could reduce that growth, and ambitious restoration could even cause the effect to shrink slightly below its 2020 potency in their analysis. This is a process we can halt if we really want to.

But since rolling all the way back to the landscape of 1800 is unlikely, elevated emissions will continue for a long time. That makes this another part of the climate system where change plays out slowly, with long-term consequences.

Nature, 2026. DOI: 10.1038/s41586-026-11339-0 ( About DOIs ).

## Winterprogramm: Stadt bittet um Sachspenden für obdachlose Menschen

Mit den kälter werdenden Temperaturen hat die Stadt Leipzig das Winterprogramm für wohnungslose Menschen wieder aufgelegt. Damit werden die Bettenkapazitäten in den Notunterkünften der Stadt hochgefahren. Parallel dazu bittet das Sozialamt um Sachspenden für Obdachlose. Was konkret benötigt wird, dazu informiert jetzt detailliert die Seite unter www.leipzig.de/obdachlos.

Martina Kador-Probst, Leiterin des Sozialamtes, sagt: „Jede Spende hilft uns, die Versorgung für wohnungslose Menschen zu verbessern. Wir danken daher allen Leipzigerinnen und Leipzigern für ihre Spendenbereitschaft und Unterstützung!“

Unter den erbetenen Sachspenden sind selbstverständlich warme Kleidung wie Socken, Unterwäsche, Mützen, Handschuhe und Schals sowie Hygieneartikel, beispielsweise Deo, Seife und Duschgel. Auch Schlafsäcke, Isomatten und Decken werden benötigt. Zudem können haltbare, abgepackte Lebensmittel gespendet werden, darunter Instant-Suppen, Kaffee-Sticks und Konserven. Die Liste führt aber auch Schüsseln, Oropax, Handtaschenwärmer und Badeschlappen auf.

Die Spenden können täglich von 9:30 bis 13 Uhr sowie von 15 bis 18 Uhr direkt in folgenden Einrichtungen abgegeben werden:

- Übernachtungshaus „Rücke“, Rückmarsdorfer Straße 5–7
- Übernachtungshaus „Helene“, Helenenstraße 26
- „Alternative I“, Chopinstraße 13
Kleidung und Gebrauchsgegenstände sollten sauber und gut erhalten sein, Unterwäsche und Hygieneartikel werden ausschließlich neu entgegengenommen.

Weitere Informationen zum Winterprogramm gibt es online unter www.leipzig.de/obdachlos .

title: Form and diversity: How tumor architecture shapes colorectal cancer progression

feedText: This diversity, known as tumor heterogeneity, reduces therapeutic efficacy because cells in different states may respond differently to therapeutic interventions.
articleBody:
# Form and diversity: How tumor architecture shapes colorectal cancer progression

## Form and diversity: How tumor architecture shapes colorectal cancer progression

edited by Lisa Lock , reviewed by Robert Egan

Lisa Lock

Scientific Editor

Robert Egan

Senior Editor

This article has been reviewed according to Science X's editorial process and policies . Editors have highlighted the following attributes while ensuring the content's credibility:

fact-checked

peer-reviewed publication

proofread

Tumors are not uniform, as even cancer cells within one patient can display extremely divergent characteristics and behaviors. This diversity, known as tumor heterogeneity, reduces therapeutic efficacy because cells in different states may respond differently to therapeutic interventions.

It is known that neither genetic mutations nor classic microscopy-based tumor grading done by trained pathologists fully reflects tumor aggressiveness or predicts disease outcome. Thus, there is a strong unmet clinical need to discover interpretable strategies to predict tumor aggression and therapy response. At the same time, such studies might reveal new mechanisms of malignancy.

The Max Planck Research Group on Biophysical Regulation of Cell State Dynamics at the Max Planck Institute for Molecular Biomedicine, led by Dr. Yekaterina (Kate) Miroshnikova, has identified a key molecular pathway that drives cancer cells to adopt multiple distinct states, which ultimately fuels therapy resistance. In short, they discovered a targetable mechanism that makes tumors more diverse and aggressive. The study was published in Nature .

The interdisciplinary team of researchers included computational biologists, clinical oncologists, engineers and cancer biologists, including some from Sara Wickström's lab at the Max Planck Institute for Molecular Biomedicine and the University of Helsinki, as well as colleagues from Roche and the National Institute of Diabetes and Digestive and Kidney Diseases (NIDDK) at the National Institutes of Health.

"In biology, form is closely related to function—we show that this is also true for cancer. Pathologists have long used abnormal nuclear shapes and tissue structure to diagnose disease. Our first goal was thus to formalize the morphometric analysis of these structures in a high-throughput, fully automated approach. Our second goal was to use this quantitative data to understand why some colorectal cancers of a similar histopathological stage progress more aggressively than others, even when they appear similar under the microscope to the most trained pathologist," said Miroshnikova.

To achieve this, the team developed a machine learning tool that automatically and accurately analyzes nuclear shape and tissue architecture across thousands of patient samples. "We found that tissue structure alone was a powerful predictor of patient outcome," says Miroshnikova.

"In particular, a specific tissue pattern that we termed 'fragmented' was prevalent among high-risk patients. These regions exposed cancer cells to mechanical confinement, triggering their reprogramming into a specific aggressive cell state and showcasing the interplay between tissue form and cell function."

## The tumor's shape predicts its course

The team analyzed tissue architecture and nuclear shape in more than 25 million cells from thousands of patient tumor samples. They trained a machine learning algorithm to distinguish three architectural patterns: glandular (ordered glandular structures), solid (dense cell clusters) and fragmented (connective tissue intermingling with tumor cell clusters).

Patients with high levels of fragmented architecture had the worst survival rates. "Even when we accounted for standard factors such as tumor stage, grade and tumor budding, the architecture alone could reliably separate patients into high- and low-risk groups," said Dr. Fabien Bertillot, the first author of the study.

"This shows that tissue structure contains vital information about disease behavior and potentially even treatment response, which is information that traditional diagnostics miss," said Bertillot.

## Fragmented architectures drive the emergence of aggressive cellular programs

On the other hand, fragmented regions were enriched in regenerative, highly plastic and adaptable stem cell states. These types of stem cells are usually absent from a healthy gut and are associated with metastatic disease and a poor prognosis in colorectal cancer.

Further, another subset of tumor cells within the fragmented regions lost proper physical connections with their neighbors, thus enabling the tissue to transition from a tightly packed arrangement to a loose, mobile form that engages in abundant physical and biochemical communication with the surrounding noncancerous tissue.

"The presence of diverse cell states and increased communication with other cell types in the surrounding tissue is likely the reason why fragmented tumors are particularly aggressive," says Bertillot.

## Mechanical forces and biochemical signals shape cell behavior

To test the mechanisms underlying cell state diversification and tumor aggression, the team turned to the in vitro modeling of tumor aggression using patient-derived organoids. These three-dimensional mini-tumors can be grown in a cell culture and can recapitulate some of the tumor cell state heterogeneity observed in patients.

These analyses enabled the team to demonstrate that mechanical signals derived from tissue architecture can induce the emergence of regenerative stem cells and aggressive behavior, as observed in actual fragmented tumors from patients.

"These experiments prove that tissue architecture not only reflects but actively drives cancer aggression. The aggressive cell states that emerge can even reshape the tumor's structure, creating a self-reinforcing cycle that makes the disease harder to treat and leads to poor patient outcomes," said Miroshnikova.

## What the results might mean for clinical practice

"We set out to improve patient risk stratification by developing strategies to quantify previously unrecognized features of tumor aggressiveness in large patient tumor samples and combined this with mechanistic perturbations to gain insights into the mechanisms," said Bertillot. "This approach has important clinical applications and could potentially help guide treatment decisions in personalized medicine."

The study provides a mechanistic understanding of how cell state diversity emerges in response to the tumor's evolving tissue architecture. "By integrating the molecular and architectural features of tumors, our work provides a new way of quantifying and understanding tumor heterogeneity," said Miroshnikova.

The current results are derived from interpretable, machine-learning-guided analyses of retrospective patient cohorts. While the results are highly promising, further validation in prospective patient cohorts and in multiple clinical centers is necessary before the analysis platform can be directly deployed in clinics to support risk stratification and treatment selection.

Publication details

Yekaterina Miroshnikova, Heterogeneity co-evolves with architecture to determine colon cancer outcome, Nature (2026). DOI: 10.1038/s41586-026-11301-0 . www.nature.com/articles/s41586-026-11301-0

# Early Stone Age rock carvings in Scandinavia may have been signposts for hunting grounds

November 26, 2026 feature

## Early Stone Age rock carvings in Scandinavia may have been signposts for hunting grounds

Sandee Oster

Author

edited by Gaby Clark , reviewed by Robert Egan

Gaby Clark

Scientific Editor

Robert Egan

Senior Editor

This article has been reviewed according to Science X's editorial process and policies . Editors have highlighted the following attributes while ensuring the content's credibility:

fact-checked

trusted source

proofread

Between roughly 9,000 and 4,000 B.C., artists in ancient Scandinavia painstakingly carved large, sometimes life-size images of elk, reindeer, bears and other creatures into rock faces teetering on the edge of fjords, rivers and lakes. But their meaning has long been debated.

Now, a new study published in World Archaeology suggests these images may have served a more practical purpose. The study suggests they served as signposts, marking areas where natural crossings drew animals together or where they could be driven into dangerous rapids.

"We often want to see them [the images] as something abstract and artistic, but they can also be concrete tools being of practical value in the adjacent landscape," the study authors said in a joint statement.

## The elk marks the spot

Rock art in Scandinavia began appearing around 9,000 B.C., the study reported. Initially, it often depicted large, sometimes life-size animals, often near water or on vertical rock faces. Then, around 5,000 B.C., the images changed; they became more narrative. The images were smaller, showed figures interacting in scenes and included people.

According to the study, rather than interpreting the older images narratively, the researchers wondered whether their meaning could be gleaned from the animals' age, sex and relationship to the surrounding landscape.

To test the idea, the authors examined four ancient rock art sites located in Sweden and Norway, namely Stykket in Trøndelag and Landverk, Gärde and Duved in Jämtland, the study reported.

According to the study, images were found at natural crossings over a fjord and rivers, with animals depicted standing at the water's edge, possibly drinking, preparing to cross and even walking toward a powerful rapid that made the water risky.

The large images would have been clearly visible even from a distance, especially from water. Being near water "makes them effective road signs, of sorts, for traveling humans arriving or passing by in canoes, or following the opposite shoreline on foot in the case of rivers," the authors wrote in the study.

Together, the four sites suggest carvings may have marked strategic hunting grounds, places that left elk exposed or where they could be forced into hard currents, the study reported. At one site, Landverk, two elk had lines carved mainly over their hearts and lungs, possibly marking the spot where the animal could be killed in a single shot.

To reach these conclusions, the researchers had to go visit the sites.

"You behave more like you're in an art museum than looking at a rocky surface in the forest," Tomas Persson, associate professor at Lund University, said. "Even though familiar from the literature, you don't get a proper feel for the images until you experience them in a natural context."

The authors stress that a more shamanic reading of these images cannot be discounted.

"Importantly, this does not exclude other functions, like a connection to shamanistic (or animist) beliefs and rituals, but that is nothing that our approach can prove," the authors said.

The study suggests that some images, particularly the earliest Scandinavian art, may have had at least a partial practical function. Why images became more narrative later on remains a mystery.

"Answers to the why question are seldom straightforward in archaeology," the authors said.

"Many of the rock carvings are older than ancient Egypt or Mesopotamian art. And to understand them, without having any external clues, such as literary sources, is utterly challenging," said Michael Ranta, associate professor and research fellow at Linnaeus University. And yet he said attempting to answer them anyway "can in itself be rewarding, even if you never get full answers to your questions."

The researchers caution that they looked at only four sites, but suggest the signpost idea could be extended to other regions.

"We often want to see them [the images] as something abstract and artistic, but they can also be concrete tools being of practical value in the adjacent landscape," the study authors said in a joint statement.

## The elk marks the spot

Rock art in Scandinavia began appearing around 9,000 B.C., the study reported. Initially, it often depicted large, sometimes life-size animals, often near water or on vertical rock faces. Then, around 5,000 B.C., the images changed; they became more narrative. The images were smaller, showed figures interacting in scenes and included people.

According to the study, rather than interpreting the older images narratively, the researchers wondered whether their meaning could be gleaned from the animals' age, sex and relationship to the surrounding landscape.

To test the idea, the authors examined four ancient rock art sites located in Sweden and Norway, namely Stykket in Trøndelag and Landverk, Gärde and Duved in Jämtland, the study reported.

According to the study, images were found at natural crossings over a fjord and rivers, with animals depicted standing at the water's edge, possibly drinking, preparing to cross and even walking toward a powerful rapid that made the water risky.

The large images would have been clearly visible even from a distance, especially from water. Being near water "makes them effective road signs, of sorts, for traveling humans arriving or passing by in canoes, or following the opposite shoreline on foot in the case of rivers," the authors wrote in the study.

Together, the four sites suggest carvings may have marked strategic hunting grounds, places that left elk exposed or where they could be forced into hard currents, the study reported. At one site, Landverk, two elk had lines carved mainly over their hearts and lungs, possibly marking the spot where the animal could be killed in a single shot.

To reach these conclusions, the researchers had to go visit the sites.

"You behave more like you're in an art museum than looking at a rocky surface in the forest," Tomas Persson, associate professor at Lund University, said. "Even though familiar from the literature, you don't get a proper feel for the images until you experience them in a natural context."

The authors stress that a more shamanic reading of these images cannot be discounted.

"Importantly, this does not exclude other functions, like a connection to shamanistic (or animist) beliefs and rituals, but that is nothing that our approach can prove," the authors said.

The study suggests that some images, particularly the earliest Scandinavian art, may have had at least a partial practical function. Why images became more narrative later on remains a mystery.

"Answers to the why question are seldom straightforward in archaeology," the authors said.

"Many of the rock carvings are older than ancient Egypt or Mesopotamian art. And to understand them, without having any external clues, such as literary sources, is utterly challenging," said Michael Ranta, associate professor and research fellow at Linnaeus University. And yet he said attempting to answer them anyway "can in itself be rewarding, even if you never get full answers to your questions."

The researchers caution that they looked at only four sites, but suggest the signpost idea could be extended to other regions.
